title: Helping Pastors Shepherd Their Time Well
author: Tim Challies
summary: Challies publishes the foreword he wrote for Shepherding Time by Rush Witt and Joe Keller as his review of the book, and uses it to argue that pastoral time management is a distinct problem rather than a variant of ordinary productivity advice. He opens from wide experience, having visited churches on every inhabited continent and met pastors in world cities and in villages without electricity, and names the four things that bind them together, the last of which is a shared struggle to manage their time well. His diagnosis is structural: pastors carry an unusual combination of responsibilities and an unusual accountability structure, and a single day can require exposition, addiction counseling, a pre-marriage class, a committee chair and a deathbed prayer. He adds a second and sharper observation, that pastors doubt not only their own use of time but their parishioners' judgment of it. The recommendation is that Witt and Keller write pastor to pastor, combine biblical argument with practical planning, and frame the subject around grace rather than law. The piece functions as a short case for why generic time-management literature underserves ministry leaders.
points: The argument's leverage comes from breadth of comparison, pastors in cities and villages, with and without electricity, all reporting the same time problem.
Challies names the day's actual range of demands, from exposition to a deathbed prayer, as the reason ordinary productivity frameworks do not transfer.
He identifies a second-order burden that generic advice ignores, namely pastors' doubt that their congregations think their time was well spent.
The book is commended for treating expectations, guilt and accountability as first-class subjects alongside practical planning.
He discloses that the review is the foreword he himself wrote, which readers should weigh when reading it as an assessment.
quotes: I have been able to meet with pastors who minister in fast-paced world cities and in slow-paced rural villages. I have been able to spend time with pastors who are at the cutting edge of technology and pastors whose homes have yet to gain electricity or running water.

There are a few things that bind all of these pastors together: Their commitment to the Word of God, their commitment to prayer, their commitment to shepherding the flock, and their struggle to manage their time well.

Yet pastors face particular challenges with their time that are often not addressed by the many books, guides, and programs available to them. They have a unique collection of responsibilities and a unique structure of accountability.
On any given day they may be expected to exposit a text, counsel an addict, lead a pre-marriage class, chair a meeting, and pray at the bed of a dying man.
Few pastors feel confident that they have used their time well. And perhaps of greater concern, few pastors feel confident that their parishioners believe they have used their time well either.

Their book is a powerful combination of biblical truths and practical pointers that draws from the deep wells of ancient wisdom and the front lines of modern innovation. It avoids the heavy hand of the law to focus instead on grace.
It will challenge, inform, and instruct you in matters like expectations, guilt, accountability, and practical planning.
